KörkortGo · M09-L02 · Use energy with control
Use energy with control
Practical energy choices · Prepare and control the car. Use a timer with an installed electric
engine heater so it warms the engine when needed, without running unnecessarily long. Set it
for the intended departure using the equipment instructions and conditions; there is no
universal heating duration. Gagnef municipal energy advice: heater timer
Air conditioning consumes energy, but it can support comfort, alertness and clear windows.
Avoid unnecessary cooling while keeping those safety benefits. Use the car's appropriate
demisting controls; visibility takes priority over a saving. Cooling is not a remedy for sleep
deprivation: stop and rest if drowsy. Revisit M07-L01 for seeing clearly and M07-L03 for attention.
NZ Transport Agency: cooling, alertness and demisting
In a conventional manual car, choose a suitably high gear in which the engine runs smoothly
without labouring. Change down if the load or gradient makes that gear unsuitable. Engine
braking means slowing with the accelerator released while a suitable gear remains engaged; do
not disengage the drive by pressing the clutch or selecting neutral for this technique. Use the
brakes whenever safety requires. Actual engine control varies, so this definition does not
promise zero fuel use or a universal RPM. Official vehicle agency: comfortable gear choice and
in-gear deceleration
Unnecessary carried mass increases the demands on the vehicle. Unload heavy equipment you
no longer need before future journeys, while retaining necessary safety and access equipment.
Removing cargo is a different check from removing a roof box's air resistance. Swedish public
energy advice: minimise weight
Apply before departure. Remove unused heavy equipment, schedule the heater for the trip, and
keep effective demisting. On an uphill section, use the gear the car can comfortably handle; a
high gear that strains the engine is not the intended economical technique.

KörkortGo · M09-L02 · Illustration
Look ahead and preserve room
The teal car approaches a queue on the right side of the road. Look ahead, retain room to stop and keep the crossing
clear. The illustration does not specify a measured following distance.
Worked decision. You can see that a traffic queue is stationary ahead. You check behind and
begin a controlled reduction in speed early, retaining enough room to stop. You do not
accelerate simply to close the gap, and you do not roll into a crossing to preserve momentum.

teaching_evidence.passage:
KörkortGo · M09-L01 · Compare powertrains and washing
Compare powertrains and washing
Powertrain and washing · Check the boundary. A battery-electric car uses only electricity for
propulsion and has no combustion tailpipe exhaust while driving. That does not remove impacts
from vehicle/battery production, raw-material extraction or electricity supply. Tyre and road
wear still matter. A plug-in hybrid combines electric and combustion operation and its traction
battery can be charged externally. A conventional non-plug-in hybrid cannot be charged from an
external electricity supply. Trafikverket: electric cars and hybrid types
Choose a purpose-built automatic or self-service wash that collects and treats its wastewater.
Washing on an ordinary street or driveway can carry oil, metals and cleaning chemicals into
ground or surface water. Treatment reduces the problem but does not remove every pollutant.
Follow the facility's product instructions and local water-protection rules. Göteborg
environmental authority: washing and treatment
Apply the comparison. A catalyst-equipped petrol car still releases fossil CO₂. An electric car
avoids combustion exhaust on that drive, but needs a broader production-and-energy
comparison. For either car, choose washing by how the dirty water is handled, rather than
assuming a mild detergent makes street runoff harmless.
Worked decision. Two vehicles are advertised using different environmental measures. One
figure describes exhaust emissions under a test procedure; another describes noise. The learner
does not rank them as though both figures measure the same thing. They first identify the
question being answered and the information still missing.

KörkortGo · M08-L04
M08-L04
Know what assistance cannot do
Your goal: Explain why safety systems and powertrain differences do not remove your
duties to observe and control.
Trafikverket describes modern protection as including crashworthiness and systems such as
lane assistance and automatic emergency braking. These functions can help, but a good safety
rating is not a promise that any collision can be avoided. Recent official crash testing also shows
the limits of automatic braking in severe truck-trailer collision scenarios. Crash safety ·
Trafikverket: braking and truck-trailer tests
ABS is anti-lock braking. It helps retain the ability to develop steering and braking forces
together, within available friction. Stability control reduces the risk of skid crashes; it does not
create extra road grip or excuse excessive speed. The driver still has to maintain control and an
appropriate speed. VTI friction report, section 4.3 · Trafikverket: tyre and stability advice · Traffic
Regulation, chapter 3 §14
Powertrain awareness. A plug-in hybrid can operate on electricity and with a combustion
engine. That difference matters when interpreting fuel use and emissions: do not assume that
every journey is electrically powered. Transportstyrelsen: plug-in hybrids
For the actual vehicle, establish how it becomes ready to move, how drive and reverse are
selected, how it is secured, and what warnings or assistance limitations need attention. Do not
transfer a universal gear-change, engine-speed, coasting or brake-check recipe between
manual, automatic, hybrid and electric vehicles. Vehicle-specific procedures need the vehicle's
own instructions and practical teaching. The curriculum's role is to help you identify those
questions, not guess their answers.

KörkortGo · M09-L03
M09-L03
Choose the journey as well as the car
Your goal: Compare combining trips, walking, cycling, public transport and driving for a
realistic personal journey.
The syllabus includes transport choices and the way personal circumstances influence them. A
useful comparison recognises that people's access needs, schedules and available services
differ. Category B syllabus, chapters 4–5
Learning approach. Start with the purpose: reaching work, collecting goods, accompanying a
person or making a visit. Then list workable options. Could two errands be combined? Could a
nearby trip be walked or cycled safely? Is public transport available for both directions? If you
share a car journey, can everyone use the required protection and travel without creating a
rushed schedule?
Do not replace one unrealistic assumption with another. A route may be short but inaccessible to
a particular person. A service may run outward but not at the return time. A car may solve those

KörkortGo · M09-L02 · Use energy with control
Use energy with control
Practical energy choices · Prepare and control the car. Use a timer with an installed electric
engine heater so it warms the engine when needed, without running unnecessarily long. Set it
for the intended departure using the equipment instructions and conditions; there is no
universal heating duration. Gagnef municipal energy advice: heater timer
Air conditioning consumes energy, but it can support comfort, alertness and clear windows.
Avoid unnecessary cooling while keeping those safety benefits. Use the car's appropriate
demisting controls; visibility takes priority over a saving. Cooling is not a remedy for sleep
deprivation: stop and rest if drowsy. Revisit M07-L01 for seeing clearly and M07-L03 for attention.
NZ Transport Agency: cooling, alertness and demisting
In a conventional manual car, choose a suitably high gear in which the engine runs smoothly
without labouring. Change down if the load or gradient makes that gear unsuitable. Engine
braking means slowing with the accelerator released while a suitable gear remains engaged; do
not disengage the drive by pressing the clutch or selecting neutral for this technique. Use the
brakes whenever safety requires. Actual engine control varies, so this definition does not
promise zero fuel use or a universal RPM. Official vehicle agency: comfortable gear choice and
in-gear deceleration
Unnecessary carried mass increases the demands on the vehicle. Unload heavy equipment you
no longer need before future journeys, while retaining necessary safety and access equipment.
Removing cargo is a different check from removing a roof box's air resistance. Swedish public
energy advice: minimise weight
Apply before departure. Remove unused heavy equipment, schedule the heater for the trip, and
keep effective demisting. On an uphill section, use the gear the car can comfortably handle; a
high gear that strains the engine is not the intended economical technique.

KörkortGo · M03-L04
M03-L04
Leave room to respond
Your goal: Explain how observation, speed, reaction, braking, grip and following space
affect your options.
Requirements. Choose a speed that preserves control and lets you stop within the road you can
see and before a foreseeable obstruction. Your distance from the vehicle ahead must allow for it
slowing or stopping. Weather, visibility, road condition, vehicle condition and loading all matter.
Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§2 and 14–16
For an ordinary car, the general speed limits are 50 km/h within a built-up area and 70 km/h
outside it, unless another applicable limit has been prescribed. The motorway default is 110
km/h; 120 km/h can be prescribed. Local and road-specific limits often differ, and a lower
vehicle-combination limit still applies. Read the current signs and conditions rather than
selecting a speed from the road’s appearance. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §17, chapter 4 §20
and chapter 9 §1
Limits and road regimes
Numeric maximum-speed examples are independent. Start and end types are labelled individually; unequal values
do not form a sequence.
C31 · Maximum speed
Hastighetsbegränsning
Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone
does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require
a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 30:
maximum 30 km/h.
Transportstyrelsen · official description

KörkortGo · M03-L04 · Continued
Continue the learning
Illustrative calculation, not a stopping-distance prediction. A speed of 50 km/h is
approximately 13.9 metres per second: 50 ÷ 3.6. If a hypothetical response delay is one second,
that is about 14 metres before braking begins. At 80 km/h the same assumed delay consumes
about 22 metres. These figures are unit conversions using an assumed delay; people do not all
react in one second, and braking distance has not yet been added.
Learning approach. Scan far enough ahead to see developing situations, while revisiting the
near area, mirrors and places where someone may enter. Avoid staring at one hazard until
everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A
timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every
condition.
Safety advice · Check a timed gap. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a
fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start
counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point.
Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly
and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor
grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing
the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method
Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one
thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on
“two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents
60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without
requiring you to estimate metres by eye.

KörkortGo · M10-L04
M10-L04
Make a realistic readiness plan
Your goal: Compare knowledge, practical performance and confidence, then plan further
learning and accessible examination preparation.
The official theory test covers vehicle knowledge/manoeuvring, environment, road safety, traffic
rules and personal factors. It checks understanding across those areas; memorising the wording
of practice questions is not equivalent preparation. The practical test requires you to apply
knowledge through vehicle checks, manoeuvres and driving in traffic. Trafikverket: category B
tests · Practical test
Current standard theory-test format, checked 1 October 2026: 70 questions, of which 65 count
towards the score; at least 52 points are needed to pass; standard time is 50 minutes. These
administrative figures can change, so verify them before booking. They are not a recommended
pass mark for this book's short learning checks. Trafikverket: theory-test format
Trafikverket provides language options, including English, and application routes for support
such as extended time, oral support or an interpreter where appropriate. Support generally
needs approval before the supported test can be booked. Check the current requirements and
apply early enough for a decision; do not assume that support can be added at the door.
Languages · Test support
Learning approach. Review three kinds of evidence: Can you explain the rule and its exceptions?
Can you recognise the situation without a prompt? Can you act safely and consistently during
supervised practice? A high confidence rating with little evidence is a learning signal, not a
readiness certificate.
Write your next practice plan in concrete terms: “Recognise cycle passages after a turn and
explain the duty before reaching them,” or “Demonstrate the safety check and explain each
defect response.” Revisit errors after a delay and in a changed scenario so that you are practising
understanding rather than recognising an answer.
Worked decision. A learner answers most checks correctly but still needs reminders to scan at
junctions. They continue targeted supervised practice instead of treating their theory score as
proof of practical readiness.

KörkortGo · M06-L01
M06-L01
Read the rural road
Your goal: Identify risks from bends, crests, narrow roads, animals and slow vehicles and
justify speed and position changes.
Requirements. Keep right when meeting another vehicle and leave a safe lateral gap. If an
obstruction on your side prevents a safe meeting, stop if necessary to let the approaching
vehicle pass. Your speed must suit the visible road and foreseeable hazards, with particular care
at bends, crests and narrow meetings. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§14–15 and 30
Learning approach. Read the road in sections: the visible straight, the entry to a bend, the
portion hidden behind a crest and the next place someone might join. Never extend the clear
section in your imagination. A vehicle emerging from a field or a cyclist beyond a bend changes
what seemed to be an empty road.
Read the rural road ahead
Independent examples of bends, gradients, narrowings, uneven road and passing places. Gradient numbers are
percentages, not a safe-speed formula.
Bends and gradients
A1 · Dangerous bend
Varning för farlig kurva
A hazardous bend lies ahead. The symbol shows its direction;
adjust speed before entering it. Left bend.

KörkortGo · M04-L02 · Waiting to turn left
Wait before steering
Safety advice · Wait with front wheels straight. When stopped waiting to turn left across
oncoming traffic, keep your front wheels pointing straight ahead. Your indicator communicates
the intended turn; your wheels do not need to point along that intended route while you wait. If
a vehicle hits you from behind, front wheels already turned left can direct the pushed car into
oncoming traffic. Keeping them straight helps reduce that risk, but cannot guarantee protection
in a collision. Begin steering into the turn only when there is a safe opportunity to make it. New
York DMV: waiting to turn left
Waiting is different from turning. Follow the positioning, signalling and observation
requirements above. The wheel-position advice does not create permission to enter or block a
junction, ignore a signal, or obstruct someone else's path. Continue observing oncoming traffic,
the receiving road, crossings and vehicles behind you while waiting. Recheck the full path before
moving.
Practice example. Sami is stopped in a suitable position, signalling left while oncoming cars
pass. A passenger suggests turning the wheels left now to be ready. Sami keeps them straight:
preparing the intention is different from starting the movement. Once the gap and receiving road
permit a safe turn, he moves and steers into it. On rural roads, use M06-L01 to assess bends,
crests and other risks before choosing a turning opportunity.

KörkortGo · M06-L01 · Rural decisions
Plan turns and read animal cues
Turn planning · Choose a safer approach. On an ordinary two-way rural road, heavy traffic may
make a direct left turn unsafe. Continue to a suitable, permitted place or route where you can
change direction safely, then return to approach the destination with a right turn if that
movement is allowed and safe. This can avoid hazardous waiting and crossing the opposing
stream at the original entrance. It is a planning alternative, not permission to turn around
immediately on the carriageway. If no safe legal return route exists, choose another route or
postpone. Trafikverket: example of routing to a turning place
Legal boundary. Before turning or leaving the road, protect oncoming traffic and traffic on the
road you enter; take particular care of following traffic. A turnaround must cause neither danger
nor obstruction. Signs and access restrictions still apply. Never turn around or reverse on a
motorway or expressway. If you can wait safely and legally for a left turn, remember the advice in
M04-L02 to keep the front wheels straight; that advice does not make an unsafe turn suitable.
Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§24, 26, 29 and 46; chapter 9 §§1–2
Worked rural alternative. A farm entrance is on your left and busy traffic leaves no safe
opportunity. You continue to an accessible junction route that legally and safely brings you back
in the opposite direction. The entrance is then on your right. Check people, traffic and the
entrance again before turning; the revised route does not guarantee a safe final movement.
Wildlife observation · Time and terrain. Give extra attention at dawn and dusk, near animal
habitats and where fences end or have openings. Scan woodland edges, bushes and small
waterways beside the road: Trafikverket's road-project study describes these as animal routes
that can conceal an approach. Its national guidance also describes animal passages through
fence openings. These are cues for observation and speed planning, not predictions that animals
only cross there. Trafikverket: wildlife and fence passages · Trafikverket: habitat example, page 9
Apply the cues. At dusk, woodland meets a field beside a gap in the fence. Read the edges and
opening as possible animal approaches, and choose speed for the view and foreseeable hazard.
Keep observing even on fenced stretches. Prevention belongs here; actions after a wildlife
collision are in M10-L02.

approximately 13.9 metres per second: 50 ÷ 3.6. If a hypothetical response delay is one second,
that is about 14 metres before braking begins. At 80 km/h the same assumed delay consumes
about 22 metres. These figures are unit conversions using an assumed delay; people do not all
react in one second, and braking distance has not yet been added.
Learning approach. Scan far enough ahead to see developing situations, while revisiting the
near area, mirrors and places where someone may enter. Avoid staring at one hazard until
everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A
timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every
condition.
Safety advice · Check a timed gap. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a
fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start
counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point.
Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly
and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor
grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing
the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method
Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one
thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on
“two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents
60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without
requiring you to estimate metres by eye.

KörkortGo · M03-L04 · Time and braking distance
Margins and braking distance
Safety advice · When someone follows too closely. Increase your gap to the vehicle ahead
gradually, allowing you to ease off and brake more gently if traffic slows. This gives the following
driver more time to respond. Do not brake sharply to warn or punish them, or accelerate into an
unsafe speed. If an emergency requires braking, brake as necessary; this advice does not mean
withholding it. Northern Ireland government: tailgater response
Tailgater example. Maya has a close follower and sees brake lights farther ahead. She eases off
early to create room in front and slows progressively. She cannot control the follower, but she
can reduce the need for a sudden stop.
Physical explanation · Twice the speed. With the same effective grip and braking deceleration
on the same gradient, braking distance is approximately proportional to speed squared: 2 ×
speed → 4 × braking distance. In a constant-deceleration model, distance = speed² ÷ (2 ×
deceleration), with speed in metres per second. Doubling speed multiplies the numerator by
four. Real conditions and brake response can change; this is a comparison under stated
assumptions. Trafikverket: VGU braking-distance equation
Hypothetical comparison. Assume a level road, unchanged vehicle/load/grip, constant braking
deceleration of 5 m/s² and a one-second response delay. At 40 km/h, braking distance is about
12.3 m and reaction distance 11.1 m. At 80 km/h they are 49.4 m and 22.2 m: braking quadruples
while reaction distance doubles. Total stopping distances are about 23.5 m and 71.6 m, so the
total does not quadruple. These invented model conditions explain the relationship; they are
not predicted stopping distances for your car.

M03-L04
Leave room to respond
Your goal: Explain how observation, speed, reaction, braking, grip and following space
affect your options.
Requirements. Choose a speed that preserves control and lets you stop within the road you can
see and before a foreseeable obstruction. Your distance from the vehicle ahead must allow for it
slowing or stopping. Weather, visibility, road condition, vehicle condition and loading all matter.
Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§2 and 14–16
For an ordinary car, the general speed limits are 50 km/h within a built-up area and 70 km/h
outside it, unless another applicable limit has been prescribed. The motorway default is 110
km/h; 120 km/h can be prescribed. Local and road-specific limits often differ, and a lower
vehicle-combination limit still applies. Read the current signs and conditions rather than
selecting a speed from the road’s appearance. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §17, chapter 4 §20
and chapter 9 §1
Limits and road regimes
Numeric maximum-speed examples are independent. Start and end types are labelled individually; unequal values
do not form a sequence.

Hastighetsbegränsning

a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 30:

KörkortGo · M05-L01
M05-L01
See the person behind the movement
Your goal: Anticipate the needs of different road users without assuming that everyone
sees, hears or moves as you do.
Requirements. Show particular consideration for children, older people, school patrols and
people whose disability or illness is apparent and affects their use of traffic. Reduce speed
appropriately near children, stopped passenger transport and other situations with foreseeable
risks. Give pedestrians sufficient room and time when meeting or passing them. Traffic
Regulation, chapter 2 §1 and chapter 3 §§15 and 58
Learning approach. Look for the space a person needs, not only the space they occupy now. A
child may be hidden by a parked car. A cyclist may need to move out from an obstruction. A
wheelchair user may need a usable kerb transition. You cannot reliably infer someone's hearing,
vision or intentions from a quick glance. Allow time and observe their movement rather than
demanding a response through the horn.
Observe people and possible movement
Children, cyclists and riders have different needs. Sensory-impairment panels are separate examples; absence of a
sign does not prove absence of risk.

KörkortGo · M06-L02
M06-L02
Is passing worth the risk?
Your goal: Compare waiting with overtaking using visibility, speed difference, space and a
safe completion path.
Requirements. Overtake only without danger and with sufficient clear road. Do not start when a
following driver has begun overtaking, or pass on the left when the vehicle ahead signals an
intended leftward movement. Leave safe lateral clearance and a safe return opportunity. When
being overtaken, do not increase speed or otherwise make the pass harder. Traffic Regulation,
chapter 3 §§31–38
The normal passing side is left. Exceptions include a vehicle turning or clearly preparing to turn
left, and the specified rules for marked same-direction lanes on roads limited to 70 km/h or less.
Passing in queues or destination lanes has separate provisions; it does not remove the need to
protect people at crossings. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§7, 31 and 41–42
Restrictions to recognise. Overtaking is generally prohibited immediately before or in a road
junction, with specified exceptions for right-side overtaking, police/signal control, or an
established yielding/stopping duty on the crossing road. Similar restrictions apply at level
crossings, with exceptions for barriers or road-junction-type traffic signals. At an obscured bend
or crest, do not use an opposing lane to overtake; the detailed provision contains limited
exceptions. Section 39 also contains an exception for passing two-wheeled vehicles without
sidecars. That exception does not override the danger prohibition, continuous-line restrictions
or the uncontrolled-crossing prohibition. None of these exceptions proves a manoeuvre safe.
Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §39
Do not overtake immediately before or on an uncontrolled pedestrian crossing, uncontrolled
cycle passage or cycle crossing. Where parallel-lane passing is legally not classified as
overtaking, the special crossing rule still requires a speed allowing an immediate stop for a
person on the crossing or passage. Obey signs and continuous-line restrictions as well. Traffic
Regulation, chapter 3 §§11, 40–41

KörkortGo · M06-L02 · Illustration
Assess the whole passing path
Learning approach. Before moving, identify the full pass and return path, not merely the first
gap. If completing it depends on another driver braking or on exceeding the limit, decline it.
Small apparent time savings are not a reason to consume every margin. Trafikverket: speed and
journey time
Following a slower vehicle towards a hidden bend. The visible straight does not establish a complete pass and
return path. The depicted spacing is illustrative, not a recommended following distance.
Worked decision. A vehicle ahead travels slightly slower than you want. An approaching bend
hides the final part of the pass. You stay behind at a useful distance. The first few clear metres do
not establish a complete overtaking opportunity.

KörkortGo · Answers and review guidance
Review after answering
M06-L01
Answer: (1) No. The view is limited; choose speed and position for that uncertainty. (2) Continue
to a suitable permitted turning place or route, change direction safely and return for a right turn
if allowed and safe. If no such route exists, choose another route or postpone. Do not make an
immediate unsafe turnaround. (3) Dawn/dusk, animal habitats such as woodland edges and
bushes, and fence endings/openings. Animals can also appear elsewhere and at other times.
M06-L02
Answer: No. Reassess and take the safest available action; do not treat finishing as more
important than avoiding a collision. Plan with enough margin that abandoning is possible before
committing.
M06-L03
Answer: (1) No. Use the lower applicable road/vehicle limit and reduce further for conditions. (2)
Perception may have adapted to the motorway pace. Check the speedometer and current limit,
then adapt to visibility and hazards. Feeling slow alone does not prove a faulty instrument or
justify accelerating.
M06-L04
Answer: Evacuate people, get away from the railway and call 112. A disabled vehicle and a
vehicle still able to drive through a barrier require different responses.
M06-R
Review guide: A complete overtaking path, a safe entry gap, current temporary instructions and
clear space beyond the tracks matter more than maintaining progress.

Check your understanding
Knowledge check. Your engine fails while the car is on the tracks. Is the priority to protect the
car or to evacuate and call for help?

KörkortGo · M07-L02
M07-L02
Grip is a changing resource
Your goal: Explain how surface conditions, tyres and driver inputs affect stability, steering
and braking.
Tyres need friction to change the vehicle's speed and direction. Braking while cornering shares
that capacity; ABS can help preserve steering forces during braking, but the available friction still
limits the result. Water, snow and ice change the conditions at the tyre contact, so dry-road
expectations cannot simply be carried into them. VTI friction report, sections 4.2–4.3
Warnings about grip
Independent slippery-road and loose-chippings warnings. Observe the actual surface; these warnings are not
limited to winter.
A10 · Slippery road
Varning för slirig väg
The road may be slippery. Do not assume that the warning
refers only to snow or ice. Skidding car inside a red-bordered
yellow triangle.
Transportstyrelsen · official description
A11 · Loose chippings
Varning för stenskott
There is a risk of stones being thrown up. This warning is not
normally used where that risk is routine, such as a gravel road.
Car wheel throws stones inside a warning triangle.
Transportstyrelsen · official description

KörkortGo · M07-L02 · Illustration
Prepare before grip changes
Learning approach. Reduce speed and increase space before reaching uncertain grip. Avoid
demanding abrupt braking, steering and acceleration together. Do not experiment with skid
recovery in ordinary traffic. Establish the actual vehicle's emergency-braking behaviour through
appropriate instruction and risk training. Trafikverket: winter driving advice · Risk training
A dry-looking foreground leads towards a shaded winter bend. The surface appearance is a reason to reassess, not a
measurement of friction. No skid-recovery technique or guaranteed tyre performance is shown.
Worked decision. Your car has suitable winter tyres, but the next bend is partly shaded and looks
different from the road behind. You reduce speed before the bend and preserve margin.
Equipment does not establish the grip at that particular point.

KörkortGo · M07-L02 · Read changing surfaces
Read changing surfaces
Surface change · A bridge can freeze first. A bridge is exposed to cold air above and below. That
exposure can cool it faster than neighbouring road supported by ground, so moisture can freeze
on the bridge while the approach still appears clear. It is a possibility, not a rule that every bridge
always freezes first. Anticipate uncertain grip and reduce speed before reaching the bridge.
National Weather Service: bridge cooling
Rain on a cold road · Ice can hide. Rainwater can freeze when it meets a road surface cold
enough for ice to form, producing a thin, nearly invisible slippery layer. The road may look wet,
and the air temperature can be above zero while the surface is still below freezing. Near-zero air
alone does not prove ice, but it calls for attention to surface conditions, more space and lower
speed. Trafikverket: deceptive ice and cold roads
First rain after dry weather · Residues matter. During a dry spell, dust, dirt and oily residues can
accumulate. The first rain can mix with these contaminants and make the road unusually
slippery. Reassess speed and separation as rain starts; do not assume a light shower
immediately washes the surface clean or that a fixed time restores grip. County Fire: rain after a
dry spell
Worked surface decision. A light shower begins after dry weather as you approach a bridge in
near-freezing conditions. Plan for both wet residues and possible local ice. The clear-looking
approach does not measure the grip on the bridge.

M07-L01
Drive within what you can see
Your goal: Choose a visibility and lighting strategy for darkness, fog and glare.

hazards. Darkness does not create a separate allowance to travel beyond the distance you can
assess. Keep the required lamps on; daytime running lights alone may be insufficient when
conditions deteriorate. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§14–15 and 68–71
Another changing condition: crosswinds

KörkortGo · M07-L01 · Continued
Continue the learning
Use main beam when needed for a sufficient field of view, but not where the road is adequately
lit, where it can dazzle an approaching driver or an adjacent rail/ship operator, or at close
distance behind another vehicle. Dipped beam is the usual driving light. In fog or heavy
precipitation, front fog lights may replace dipped beam; the prohibited combinations must not
be used together. A rear fog light is restricted to fog, heavy precipitation or comparable reduced
visibility and must not dazzle a following driver. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§69–72
Learning approach. Make lighting and speed one decision. If you dip the lights and can see less
far, reassess speed immediately. Check the edges of the visible road for people and animals
rather than assuming a dark area is empty. Keep windows and mirrors clear enough for a useful
view and learn demisting controls before a difficult journey.
Automatic lighting is an aid, not confirmation that every required lamp is on. In a car whose
daytime-light mode leaves the rear lights off, check the actual setting when darkness or bad
weather arrives. Transportstyrelsen: vehicle lighting

slippery. Reassess speed and separation as rain starts; do not assume a light shower
immediately washes the surface clean or that a fixed time restores grip. County Fire: rain after a
dry spell

near-freezing conditions. Plan for both wet residues and possible local ice. The clear-looking
approach does not measure the grip on the bridge.

KörkortGo · M07-L02 · Read changing surfaces
Read changing surfaces
Surface change · A bridge can freeze first. A bridge is exposed to cold air above and below. That
exposure can cool it faster than neighbouring road supported by ground, so moisture can freeze
on the bridge while the approach still appears clear. It is a possibility, not a rule that every bridge
always freezes first. Anticipate uncertain grip and reduce speed before reaching the bridge.
National Weather Service: bridge cooling
Rain on a cold road · Ice can hide. Rainwater can freeze when it meets a road surface cold
enough for ice to form, producing a thin, nearly invisible slippery layer. The road may look wet,
and the air temperature can be above zero while the surface is still below freezing. Near-zero air
alone does not prove ice, but it calls for attention to surface conditions, more space and lower
speed. Trafikverket: deceptive ice and cold roads

KörkortGo · M05-L01 · Share the space
Share the space
Bus comparison · Check the road limit. The threshold concerns the maximum permitted speed
on the road, not how fast you happen to be travelling. At a 70 km/h limit, the special bus-stop
departure rule above does not apply. The bus must wait for an entry that can be made without
danger or unnecessary obstruction. You still have a duty to adapt speed to facilitate an observed
entry into your lane. A bus indicator does not create unconditional priority, and the higher road
limit does not excuse deliberately blocking it. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§43–45
Road limit
Duties when the bus signals to leave its stop
50 km/h or lower
Slow and let the bus leave; stop if needed. The bus driver must take
particular care.
70 km/h, ordinary entry into your lane
The special bus-exit duty does not apply. The bus waits for a safe
entry; you adapt speed to facilitate the observed entry.
Safety advice · Let a guide dog work. Do not pet, call to or talk to a working guide dog to attract
its attention. Distraction can endanger the person it is helping. Allow the pair room and time; if
you need to communicate, address the handler rather than trying to direct the dog. The handler
chooses the route and remains in control. For example, a passenger beside your parked car
wants to greet a guide dog at a crossing. Ask them to leave it working and keep the path clear.
MFD: meeting a working guide dog
Traffic terminology · A bicycle is a vehicle. A person riding an ordinary pedal bicycle is operating
a vehicle, even without an engine. “Vehicle” does not mean only “motor vehicle”. Apply the
relevant cyclist duties and protections; crossing distinctions remain in M04-L03.
Transportstyrelsen: bicycle definition

KörkortGo · M10-L02
M10-L02
When someone may be hurt
Your goal: Identify scene-safety, emergency-contact and first-aid learning needs following
a collision.
Requirements. If involved in a traffic accident, remain at the scene, help injured people to the
extent of your ability and assist with necessary measures. Provide your name, address and
information when requested by another involved person or someone whose property was
damaged. Notify the owner or police promptly if damaged property has nobody present to
receive the information. Notify police promptly for a personal injury that is not insignificant.
Traffic Regulation, chapter 2 §8
A vehicle creating danger or obstruction after a collision should be moved to a suitable place.
However, where someone has died or been seriously injured, move it only if it endangers other
traffic, and preserve evidence as required. Staying at the scene does not mean standing in an
active traffic lane. Protect yourself and others while arranging help. Traffic Regulation, chapter 2
§8
Emergency response. At danger to life, call 112. Give the location, direction of travel, what
happened and what dangers you can see; follow the operator's instructions. Make observations
from a safe position rather than walking into moving traffic to gather details. Trafikverket:
emergency contact

KörkortGo · M10-L02 · Illustration
Call from a protected place
Call from a protected place, away from traffic. For a life-threatening emergency, call 112 and describe the location,
direction of travel, what happened and immediate dangers. Follow the operator's instructions.
Worked decision. After a collision, a person is badly injured and vehicles are still passing. You
call 112 and describe the immediate traffic danger from a protected position, following
instructions and helping within your ability. Photographing damage is not the first priority.

teaching_evidence.passage:
KörkortGo · M06-L01 · Rural decisions
Plan turns and read animal cues
Turn planning · Choose a safer approach. On an ordinary two-way rural road, heavy traffic may
make a direct left turn unsafe. Continue to a suitable, permitted place or route where you can
change direction safely, then return to approach the destination with a right turn if that
movement is allowed and safe. This can avoid hazardous waiting and crossing the opposing
stream at the original entrance. It is a planning alternative, not permission to turn around
immediately on the carriageway. If no safe legal return route exists, choose another route or
postpone. Trafikverket: example of routing to a turning place
Legal boundary. Before turning or leaving the road, protect oncoming traffic and traffic on the
road you enter; take particular care of following traffic. A turnaround must cause neither danger
nor obstruction. Signs and access restrictions still apply. Never turn around or reverse on a
motorway or expressway. If you can wait safely and legally for a left turn, remember the advice in
M04-L02 to keep the front wheels straight; that advice does not make an unsafe turn suitable.
Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§24, 26, 29 and 46; chapter 9 §§1–2
Worked rural alternative. A farm entrance is on your left and busy traffic leaves no safe
opportunity. You continue to an accessible junction route that legally and safely brings you back
in the opposite direction. The entrance is then on your right. Check people, traffic and the
entrance again before turning; the revised route does not guarantee a safe final movement.
Wildlife observation · Time and terrain. Give extra attention at dawn and dusk, near animal
habitats and where fences end or have openings. Scan woodland edges, bushes and small
waterways beside the road: Trafikverket's road-project study describes these as animal routes
that can conceal an approach. Its national guidance also describes animal passages through
fence openings. These are cues for observation and speed planning, not predictions that animals
only cross there. Trafikverket: wildlife and fence passages · Trafikverket: habitat example, page 9
Apply the cues. At dusk, woodland meets a field beside a gap in the fence. Read the edges and
opening as possible animal approaches, and choose speed for the view and foreseeable hazard.
Keep observing even on fenced stretches. Prevention belongs here; actions after a wildlife
collision are in M10-L02.

Transportstyrelsen · official description
First-aid reference. Use 1177's first-aid guidance to learn more about helping someone in an
acute situation, including when a person is unconscious or has breathing difficulties. Practical
first-aid training can help you prepare. This lesson is deliberately brief and does not reproduce
clinical procedures or a pulse-check sequence. In an emergency, call 112 rather than spending
time searching a website.
Wildlife collisions. Trafikverket advises calling 112 and marking the collision location safely so
responders can find it, even if the animal has left. Avoid approaching an injured animal. Its
guidance gives a separate precaution for wild boar, bear, lynx and wolf: continue 200 m before
stopping and marking, then call police immediately. Only move the vehicle when safe and
possible; explain the actual collision location and the animal's direction clearly. This is agency
safety guidance, not a claim that every animal species has identical statutory reporting rules.

KörkortGo · M10-L01
M10-L01
When the car cannot continue
Your goal: Compare a breakdown on an ordinary road, a motorway and in a tunnel.
Requirement. If a breakdown leaves a vehicle where stopping is prohibited, it must be moved to
a suitable place as soon as possible, subject to the special rules for an accident scene. Warning
obligations depend on the situation. A warning triangle must give approaching drivers enough
warning; the law does not prescribe one universal distance for every road. Traffic Regulation,
chapter 3 §§51 and 57
Official motorway/2+1-road advice. If possible, reach the safest available stopping place.
Switch on hazard lights, warn other traffic and leave the vehicle and carriageway promptly. Move
away from traffic, outside a barrier where one exists. Trafikverket recommends placing the
triangle at least 100 m away, preferably farther, and taking care while doing so, walking at the
side and outside the barrier where possible. Do not expose yourself in the traffic lane to carry out
a roadside repair. Call professional recovery; call 112 when life is in danger. Trafikverket:
breakdown advice
Tunnel advice is different. Use hazard lights, move towards the edge or an emergency bay if
possible and switch off the engine. For a non-urgent incident, Trafikverket advises staying in the
car or protected from traffic close to it while calling for assistance. In an urgent situation, leave
for the nearest emergency exit and use the assistance point, emergency phone or 112. In a fire,
leave and reach an emergency exit; follow signs, announcements and emergency personnel. Do
not turn a non-urgent-tunnel recommendation into advice to stay beside a fire. Trafikverket:
tunnels

KörkortGo · Chapter 1
CHAPTER 01
Choose to drive responsibly
Driving begins with a choice: whether this person, this vehicle and this journey are ready to go
together. Sweden’s Vision Zero (Nollvisionen) aims for no one to be killed or seriously injured in
traffic. The choices taught here contribute to that aim. Trafikverket: Vision Zero Learning rules
matters, but so does recognising when a different plan is safer. This module helps you build both
habits.
In this chapter
M01-L01 · Your route into driving
M01-L02 · Am I ready today?
M01-L03 · Pressure is a driving risk
M01-L04 · Plan the journey before the ignition
M01-R · Review and self-assessment
Answers and review guidance
Official references
This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an
official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and
Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules.

KörkortGo · M01-L03
M01-L03
Pressure is a driving risk
Your goal: Identify how peers, impulses, confidence and personal circumstances can
change a decision, and rehearse a refusal or alternative.
The official education syllabus asks learners to reflect on social influence, impulsive decisions,
personal motives and their own limitations. These are skills to practise, not labels to attach to an
age group or personality. Category B syllabus, chapter 5
Learning approach. Separate the journey's purpose from the feeling of the moment. “Get
everyone home” is a purpose. “Show that I can handle this bend quickly” is a different motive.
When a passenger's request changes your speed, following distance or willingness to overtake,
name the change before acting on it.
A useful personal boundary is a sentence you can use without debate: “I will stop somewhere
safe before changing the route”; “I am not passing here”; or “We need another way home.” These
are original rehearsal tools, not official scripts. Practise them before a difficult situation, and
agree that passengers will help with navigation only when asked.
Requirement. You still owe care to other road users and must adapt speed to conditions.
Cooperation does not authorise ignoring a traffic rule because another person is impatient.
Traffic Regulation, chapter 2 §1 and chapter 3 §14
Official policy aim · Vision Zero. Nollvisionen means no one should be killed or seriously injured
in traffic. It is not a promise that nobody will ever make a mistake. Trafikverket describes shared
responsibility: road users must show consideration and judgement and follow traffic rules, while
system designers have ultimate responsibility for the system’s safety. Your part includes
choosing safe speed and margins and refusing a pressured manoeuvre; road and vehicle design
also contribute. For example, staying behind a vehicle near a hidden crest helps protect people
even when a passenger dislikes the delay. Trafikverket: Vision Zero

KörkortGo · M02-L03
M02-L03
Protect everyone inside
Your goal: Select suitable restraints for passengers and explain how belts, headrests and
airbags work together.
Requirements. In an ordinary car journey, occupants must use an available belt-equipped place
and wear the belt. Children under 135 cm normally need an appropriate child restraint. The
driver must take appropriate measures to ensure passengers under 15 use the required
protection. Limited exceptions exist, including specified short occasional journeys, and should
not become a routine travel plan. Seat-belt rules · Traffic Regulation, chapter 4 §§10–10d
For a child aged three or more but shorter than 135 cm, an occasional short transport without an
available child restraint is an exception only under the stated conditions: use the belt where
possible and not the front seat of a passenger car or light goods vehicle. For a child under three,
the exception is an occasional short taxi trip, also excluding the front seat. Plan with the correct
restraint instead. Transportstyrelsen: child rules
Official recommendations. Trafikverket recommends rear-facing travel until at least four to five
years, preferably longer. Transportstyrelsen's advice says as long as possible, normally around
four. These are recommendations, not a single legal birthday on which to turn the seat. Choose
equipment that fits the child and car and stays within its approved size and weight limits.
Reaching 135 cm does not automatically produce good adult-belt fit. Trafikverket: children in
cars · Transportstyrelsen: child protection
Never place a rear-facing child restraint in front of an active passenger airbag. Trafikverket
advises at least 140 cm in front of an active airbag unless the manufacturer recommends
otherwise; Transportstyrelsen gives more conservative advice for children in restraints. Resolve
seating and airbag compatibility using the vehicle and restraint instructions before travelling. An
airbag supplements a belt; it does not replace one. Adjust the head restraint for the person
occupying the seat. Children in cars · Airbags · Seats and head restraints

KörkortGo · M02-L03 · Further learning
How protection works
Technical explanation · Head restraints. In a rear impact, the seat and torso can move while the
head lags behind. A correctly designed and adjusted head restraint helps limit damaging head
movement relative to the torso and reduce neck-injury risk. Trafikverket advises positioning the
top at the crown of the head and keeping the gap behind the head as small as possible. Adjust it
for the occupant before driving; a comfort setting is not the same as a protective setting. A head
restraint cannot guarantee that injury will be avoided. Trafikverket: seats and head restraints
Why children face backwards. A young child's head is relatively heavy and the neck is
vulnerable. In a frontal collision, a rear-facing seat supports the head and body together, takes
up collision forces and distributes the load across the supported body. The neck does not have
to restrain the heavy head on its own in the same way as when facing forwards. This is why the
recommendations above concern protection, not only seat orientation. Follow the seat's size
limits, fitting instructions and airbag compatibility. Trafikverket: child head and neck protection
· Transportstyrelsen: rear-facing collision protection
Controlled deformation. Crumple zones are parts of a vehicle designed to deform progressively
in a collision, absorbing energy while the passenger compartment's structure protects the
occupants' space. Spreading the deceleration over a longer time reduces forces acting on the
people inside. A car remaining visually undamaged is not the objective: designed deformation
can be part of its protection. Belts and suitable child restraints still matter, and no structure
makes every collision survivable. Western Australia government: structure and crumple zones
Practice example. A family prepares a car for a child and an adult passenger. They check
rear-facing seat fit and airbag compatibility, and adjust the adult's head restraint. After
discussing crash protection, they recognise that the restraint, seat and deforming vehicle
structure have different roles that work together.

KörkortGo · M02-L03 · Worked decision
Apply the learning
An adult and child stand beside an open rear door. The empty booster and rear bench face forwards. This scene
does not demonstrate installation or belt fit; follow the child-restraint and vehicle instructions.
Worked decision. A child reaches the legal height threshold, but the belt still lies badly. The
adult checks an appropriate approved booster rather than treating the threshold as an
instruction to discard it.
Knowledge check. (1) Is a rear-facing seat safe in front of an active airbag for a short trip? (2)
What does a head restraint do? (3) Why does rear-facing travel protect a small child? (4) Why are
crumple zones designed to deform?
Remember: Legal minimums, official recommendations and equipment compatibility answer different questions.

teaching_evidence.passage:
KörkortGo · M05-L01 · Share the space
Share the space
Bus comparison · Check the road limit. The threshold concerns the maximum permitted speed
on the road, not how fast you happen to be travelling. At a 70 km/h limit, the special bus-stop
departure rule above does not apply. The bus must wait for an entry that can be made without
danger or unnecessary obstruction. You still have a duty to adapt speed to facilitate an observed
entry into your lane. A bus indicator does not create unconditional priority, and the higher road
limit does not excuse deliberately blocking it. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§43–45
Road limit
Duties when the bus signals to leave its stop
50 km/h or lower
Slow and let the bus leave; stop if needed. The bus driver must take
particular care.
70 km/h, ordinary entry into your lane
The special bus-exit duty does not apply. The bus waits for a safe
entry; you adapt speed to facilitate the observed entry.
Safety advice · Let a guide dog work. Do not pet, call to or talk to a working guide dog to attract
its attention. Distraction can endanger the person it is helping. Allow the pair room and time; if
you need to communicate, address the handler rather than trying to direct the dog. The handler
chooses the route and remains in control. For example, a passenger beside your parked car
wants to greet a guide dog at a crossing. Ask them to leave it working and keep the path clear.
MFD: meeting a working guide dog
Traffic terminology · A bicycle is a vehicle. A person riding an ordinary pedal bicycle is operating
a vehicle, even without an engine. “Vehicle” does not mean only “motor vehicle”. Apply the
relevant cyclist duties and protections; crossing distinctions remain in M04-L03.
Transportstyrelsen: bicycle definition

teaching_evidence.passage:
KörkortGo · M08-L01
M08-L01
Understand what you may drive
Your goal: Use entitlement and vehicle information to assess a car or trailer combination.
Requirements. Ordinary category B permits a passenger car or light goods vehicle with a total
weight of no more than 3,500 kg. For trailers, either the trailer's total weight is at most 750 kg, or,
if above 750 kg, the car and trailer's combined total weights must not exceed 3,500 kg. The first
route can therefore permit a combination up to 4,250 kg; it does not mean every 4,250 kg
combination is permitted on ordinary B. Category B · Car with trailer
Extended B (B96) permits combined total weights up to 4,250 kg, without increasing the car's
3,500 kg limit. Under the ordinary current BE rule, the towing car is still limited to 3,500 kg total
weight and the trailer or trailers may have combined total weights up to 3,500 kg. Older
entitlements and conditions can differ; check the individual licence rather than applying a
current-new-licence example to everyone. This book is not a full B96 or BE course. Trailer
entitlement guide
Two tests. Entitlement uses registered total weights. Technical towing limits also restrict what
the particular car may pull in its actual loaded state. Emptying a trailer may reduce its actual
weight without changing its registered total weight, so it may solve a technical-weight problem
but not an entitlement problem. Towing weights
Vehicle comparison · Light lorry without a trailer. A light lorry (lätt lastbil) has a registered total
weight of at most 3,500 kg. Without a trailer, it normally follows the road's maximum speed; the
general heavy-lorry cap does not apply. A heavy lorry exceeds 3,500 kg: without a trailer its
vehicle maximum is 90 km/h on a motorway or expressway, and 80 km/h on other roads; with a
trailer it is 80 km/h. A lower road limit always applies. For a light lorry towing, check the
combination rules in M08-L02. Transportstyrelsen: light and heavy lorries
Apply the limit. A light lorry without a trailer on a road signed 100 km/h does not acquire an 80
km/h cap simply because it is called a lorry. Still reduce speed for visibility, grip, traffic and load;
a maximum is not a target. Safe-speed duty, chapter 3 §14

teaching_evidence.passage:
KörkortGo · M03-L04 · Continued
Continue the learning
Illustrative calculation, not a stopping-distance prediction. A speed of 50 km/h is
approximately 13.9 metres per second: 50 ÷ 3.6. If a hypothetical response delay is one second,
that is about 14 metres before braking begins. At 80 km/h the same assumed delay consumes
about 22 metres. These figures are unit conversions using an assumed delay; people do not all
react in one second, and braking distance has not yet been added.
Learning approach. Scan far enough ahead to see developing situations, while revisiting the
near area, mirrors and places where someone may enter. Avoid staring at one hazard until
everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A
timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every
condition.
Safety advice · Check a timed gap. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a
fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start
counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point.
Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly
and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor
grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing
the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method
Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one
thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on
“two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents
60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without
requiring you to estimate metres by eye.

KörkortGo · M03-L04 · Time and braking distance
Margins and braking distance
Safety advice · When someone follows too closely. Increase your gap to the vehicle ahead
gradually, allowing you to ease off and brake more gently if traffic slows. This gives the following
driver more time to respond. Do not brake sharply to warn or punish them, or accelerate into an
unsafe speed. If an emergency requires braking, brake as necessary; this advice does not mean
withholding it. Northern Ireland government: tailgater response
Tailgater example. Maya has a close follower and sees brake lights farther ahead. She eases off
early to create room in front and slows progressively. She cannot control the follower, but she
can reduce the need for a sudden stop.
Physical explanation · Twice the speed. With the same effective grip and braking deceleration
on the same gradient, braking distance is approximately proportional to speed squared: 2 ×
speed → 4 × braking distance. In a constant-deceleration model, distance = speed² ÷ (2 ×
deceleration), with speed in metres per second. Doubling speed multiplies the numerator by
four. Real conditions and brake response can change; this is a comparison under stated
assumptions. Trafikverket: VGU braking-distance equation
Hypothetical comparison. Assume a level road, unchanged vehicle/load/grip, constant braking
deceleration of 5 m/s² and a one-second response delay. At 40 km/h, braking distance is about
12.3 m and reaction distance 11.1 m. At 80 km/h they are 49.4 m and 22.2 m: braking quadruples
while reaction distance doubles. Total stopping distances are about 23.5 m and 71.6 m, so the
total does not quadruple. These invented model conditions explain the relationship; they are
not predicted stopping distances for your car.

KörkortGo · M03-L04 · Continued
Continue the learning
Illustrative calculation, not a stopping-distance prediction. A speed of 50 km/h is
approximately 13.9 metres per second: 50 ÷ 3.6. If a hypothetical response delay is one second,
that is about 14 metres before braking begins. At 80 km/h the same assumed delay consumes
about 22 metres. These figures are unit conversions using an assumed delay; people do not all
react in one second, and braking distance has not yet been added.
Learning approach. Scan far enough ahead to see developing situations, while revisiting the
near area, mirrors and places where someone may enter. Avoid staring at one hazard until
everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A
timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every
condition.
Safety advice · Check a timed gap. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a
fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start
counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point.
Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly
and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor
grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing
the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method
Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one
thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on
“two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents
60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without
requiring you to estimate metres by eye.

KörkortGo · M07-L02
M07-L02
Grip is a changing resource
Your goal: Explain how surface conditions, tyres and driver inputs affect stability, steering
and braking.
Tyres need friction to change the vehicle's speed and direction. Braking while cornering shares
that capacity; ABS can help preserve steering forces during braking, but the available friction still
limits the result. Water, snow and ice change the conditions at the tyre contact, so dry-road
expectations cannot simply be carried into them. VTI friction report, sections 4.2–4.3
Warnings about grip
Independent slippery-road and loose-chippings warnings. Observe the actual surface; these warnings are not
limited to winter.

Requirements for ordinary light cars and their trailers, checked 1 October 2026. Between 1
December and 31 March, winter tyres or equivalent equipment are required when winter
conditions exist. Snow, ice, slush or frost on any part of the road counts; police determine
conditions at the location. The minimum tread depth for the ordinary light-vehicle case is 3 mm.
Studless winter tyres for the car need the mountain/snowflake marking. Winter tyres
Studded tyres are permitted from 1 October to 15 April and outside that period when winter
conditions exist or are expected. Do not mix studded and non-studded tyres on an ordinary
passenger car or light goods vehicle. In winter conditions, a studded towing car requires a
studded trailer; the reverse combination is allowed. A light-trailer transition permits specified
winter-designed M+S tyres through 30 November 2028. Exemptions and heavier-vehicle cases
need their own checks; they are not the ordinary car rule. Winter tyres · Traffic Regulation,
chapter 4 §§18a–18d
Check local studded-tyre restrictions
Seasonal permission to use studs does not override a local prohibition. This road sign is not a tyre sidewall marking.
C44 · No studded-tyre motor vehicles except class II mopeds
Förbud mot trafik med annat motordrivet fordon med dubbdäck
än moped klass II
The prohibition concerns motor vehicles with studded tyres.
Class II mopeds are included only if a supplementary panel
says so. Studded tyre crossed by a red diagonal.
Transportstyrelsen · official description
For summer conditions, the minimum tread depth is 1.6 mm. Transportstyrelsen recommends
placing the tyres with the best grip or greatest tread depth at the rear and checking pressure
against the vehicle's instructions. A legal minimum is not a promise of equal performance in
every condition. Transportstyrelsen: tyres

KörkortGo · M09-L02
M09-L02
Use energy with foresight
Your goal: Plan anticipatory driving that reduces unnecessary energy use while preserving
safety.
Transportstyrelsen recommends correct tyre pressure, observing speed limits and removing
unused roof racks or roof boxes. Driving technique and environmental awareness are part of
driver education and assessment. Transportstyrelsen: economical driving
Learning approach. Look ahead and respond early to a developing queue rather than
accelerating towards it and then braking sharply. Choose a suitable speed and preserve a gap
that lets you adapt smoothly. This is not an instruction to delay necessary braking: safe control
and traffic duties come first. If you need to stop for a person, do so regardless of what an
efficiency display suggests. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§2 and 14
Prepare the vehicle for the trip. Check the specified tyre pressure and remove unnecessary
external carrying equipment when it is no longer needed. Combine these habits with realistic
route and timing decisions. Avoid claiming a fixed percentage saving: load, road, weather,
vehicle and technique all affect the outcome.
Vehicle-specific boundary. Gear selection and deceleration strategies vary. Do not use a fixed
engine-speed rule for every car or assume every powertrain cuts fuel or recovers energy in the
same way. Learn the actual vehicle's approved operation with your instructor. This book does
not recommend coasting in neutral or switching the vehicle off while moving.

KörkortGo · M02-L02
M02-L02
A check before moving
Your goal: Organise a safety check of tyres, lights, visibility and vehicle condition, and
distinguish a defect from a reason to seek help.
Learning approach. Work around the car, then through the driving position. Look for damaged
tyres, an unusual stance, leaks or obstructions; confirm that windows and mirrors permit a
useful view. Check required lights and indicators, and ask for help where a second person is
useful. Check washers and wipers before you need them in poor weather. Use the actual
vehicle's instructions for fluid levels and service checks. These groups reflect the official
practical-test safety check; they are not a guarantee that a quick walkaround detects every
defect. Trafikverket: safety check
Requirements. Tyres must be suitable for the vehicle, including load capacity and applicable
speed capability. The registration information and approved vehicle requirements matter when
changing tyre sizes. Do not assume any wheel that physically fits is suitable. Transportstyrelsen:
tyre requirements
Required lighting must work and be used appropriately. Some cars can run daytime lights
without rear lights; the driver must ensure suitable front, rear and side lighting is on in darkness,
twilight or poor weather. A trailer's lighting must be on during travel. Automatic settings may
need manual intervention. Transportstyrelsen: vehicle lighting
Technical explanation · Steering vibration. Uneven mass distribution around a rotating wheel
and tyre can cause steering vibration, sometimes most noticeable at particular speeds. Wheel
imbalance is one possible cause, not a diagnosis: tyre damage and other wheel or steering
defects may also be involved. Arrange assessment rather than testing the symptom by driving
faster. Northern Ireland government: wheel balance and vehicle faults
Vehicle instructions · A temporary spare. Before using a temporary spare, read the actual car
and spare-wheel instructions for maximum speed, distance or use restrictions, and required tyre
pressure. Follow those limits and replace it with the normal wheel as instructed. Its pressure can
differ from the road tyres. Volvo's 2019 V60 Twin Engine handbook gives one model's
temporary-use, speed and pressure requirements; these cannot be assumed for every car. Volvo:
temporary spare, 2019 V60 Twin Engine

KörkortGo · M07-L02 · Understand grip and handling
Understand grip and handling
Rear stability · Why the best grip belongs at the rear. Transportstyrelsen recommends the
best-grip or deepest-tread tyres at the rear to reduce skid risk in braking and bends, for both
front- and rear-wheel-drive cars. Better rear grip helps reduce the risk of the rear sliding outward
and rotating the car. Suitable tyres and stability assistance still cannot guarantee control.
Transportstyrelsen: best tyres at the rear · VTI: rear grip and oversteer
Oversteer · Rear grip loss. In the loss-of-grip situation, the rear tyres lose sufficient lateral grip,
the tail swings outward and the car rotates more than intended into the turn. This can develop
into a spin. VTI: oversteer and rear stability
Understeer · Front grip loss. In the loss-of-grip situation, the front tyres cannot supply the
lateral grip needed for the requested turn. The car turns less than intended and follows a
straighter, wider path; adding more steering does not guarantee the requested curve. These are
grip-loss explanations, not a full definition of every vehicle's normal handling characteristics.
VTI: handling paths · NHTSA: front-axle grip limit
Aquaplaning · Water interrupts contact. If water builds between tyres and road, it can support
the tyre on a film and reduce or remove effective tyre-road contact. Steering and braking then
have less grip to work with. Reduce speed before standing water and uncertain wet surfaces.
PennDOT: aquaplaning
Response · Ease off smoothly. If aquaplaning starts and there is space to slow gradually, ease off
the accelerator, keep steering steady and avoid abrupt steering or hard braking. Make only
gentle necessary corrections as contact returns. This is different from M02-L01's ABS
emergency-stop instruction: ABS cannot create grip where a tyre is separated from the road by
water. An immediate collision emergency needs action appropriate to the actual situation; this
advice does not establish a universal ban on braking. PennDOT: aquaplaning response
Worked grip comparison. A rear slide swinging the tail outward is oversteer; a front slide that
prevents the intended curve is understeer. A light, unresponsive steering feel over standing
water raises a different possibility: aquaplaning. Recognise the mechanism, preserve margins
and practise vehicle-specific emergency handling only with suitable instruction.

teaching_evidence.passage:
KörkortGo · M08-L04
M08-L04
Know what assistance cannot do
Your goal: Explain why safety systems and powertrain differences do not remove your
duties to observe and control.
Trafikverket describes modern protection as including crashworthiness and systems such as
lane assistance and automatic emergency braking. These functions can help, but a good safety
rating is not a promise that any collision can be avoided. Recent official crash testing also shows
the limits of automatic braking in severe truck-trailer collision scenarios. Crash safety ·
Trafikverket: braking and truck-trailer tests
ABS is anti-lock braking. It helps retain the ability to develop steering and braking forces
together, within available friction. Stability control reduces the risk of skid crashes; it does not
create extra road grip or excuse excessive speed. The driver still has to maintain control and an
appropriate speed. VTI friction report, section 4.3 · Trafikverket: tyre and stability advice · Traffic
Regulation, chapter 3 §14
Powertrain awareness. A plug-in hybrid can operate on electricity and with a combustion
engine. That difference matters when interpreting fuel use and emissions: do not assume that
every journey is electrically powered. Transportstyrelsen: plug-in hybrids
For the actual vehicle, establish how it becomes ready to move, how drive and reverse are
selected, how it is secured, and what warnings or assistance limitations need attention. Do not
transfer a universal gear-change, engine-speed, coasting or brake-check recipe between
manual, automatic, hybrid and electric vehicles. Vehicle-specific procedures need the vehicle's
own instructions and practical teaching. The curriculum's role is to help you identify those
questions, not guess their answers.

KörkortGo · M02-L01 · Further learning
Brakes and protective circuits
Technical explanation · Brakes and electrical protection. Separate brake circuits provide a
reserve: if one circuit fails, the remaining circuit can still provide some braking. This reduces the
chance of losing all braking through one circuit fault. Remaining braking may be weaker; it is not
permission to continue normally. The technical requirements distinguish the surviving capability
from full service-brake performance. Transportstyrelsen: brake circuits
ABS in an emergency. Anti-lock braking helps prevent wheel locking and can preserve steering
control. During an emergency stop with ABS, keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal
and steer as necessary; do not pump the pedal. Pulsation or vibration through the pedal during
ABS operation can be normal feedback as the system regulates braking. This differs from a
changed pedal feel in ordinary braking. ABS does not guarantee a shorter stop or create grip that
the tyres lack. UK Government: ABS instruction, Rule 120 · Ford: normal ABS feedback, 2011
Explorer
Recognise a symptom, then act. The table gives possibilities, not diagnoses. A sinking pedal can
suggest internal leakage, although some servo/pump behaviour can resemble it. Air can cause
hydraulic pedal sponginess. Obtain professional assessment for an unexplained change.

Brakes and protective circuits
Technical explanation · Brakes and electrical protection. Separate brake circuits provide a
reserve: if one circuit fails, the remaining circuit can still provide some braking. This reduces the
chance of losing all braking through one circuit fault. Remaining braking may be weaker; it is not
permission to continue normally. The technical requirements distinguish the surviving capability
from full service-brake performance. Transportstyrelsen: brake circuits
ABS in an emergency. Anti-lock braking helps prevent wheel locking and can preserve steering
control. During an emergency stop with ABS, keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal
and steer as necessary; do not pump the pedal. Pulsation or vibration through the pedal during
ABS operation can be normal feedback as the system regulates braking. This differs from a
changed pedal feel in ordinary braking. ABS does not guarantee a shorter stop or create grip that
the tyres lack. UK Government: ABS instruction, Rule 120 · Ford: normal ABS feedback, 2011

teaching_evidence.passage:
KörkortGo · M02-L03 · Further learning
How protection works
Technical explanation · Head restraints. In a rear impact, the seat and torso can move while the
head lags behind. A correctly designed and adjusted head restraint helps limit damaging head
movement relative to the torso and reduce neck-injury risk. Trafikverket advises positioning the
top at the crown of the head and keeping the gap behind the head as small as possible. Adjust it
for the occupant before driving; a comfort setting is not the same as a protective setting. A head
restraint cannot guarantee that injury will be avoided. Trafikverket: seats and head restraints
Why children face backwards. A young child's head is relatively heavy and the neck is
vulnerable. In a frontal collision, a rear-facing seat supports the head and body together, takes
up collision forces and distributes the load across the supported body. The neck does not have
to restrain the heavy head on its own in the same way as when facing forwards. This is why the
recommendations above concern protection, not only seat orientation. Follow the seat's size
limits, fitting instructions and airbag compatibility. Trafikverket: child head and neck protection
· Transportstyrelsen: rear-facing collision protection
Controlled deformation. Crumple zones are parts of a vehicle designed to deform progressively
in a collision, absorbing energy while the passenger compartment's structure protects the
occupants' space. Spreading the deceleration over a longer time reduces forces acting on the
people inside. A car remaining visually undamaged is not the objective: designed deformation
can be part of its protection. Belts and suitable child restraints still matter, and no structure
makes every collision survivable. Western Australia government: structure and crumple zones
Practice example. A family prepares a car for a child and an adult passenger. They check
rear-facing seat fit and airbag compatibility, and adjust the adult's head restraint. After
discussing crash protection, they recognise that the restraint, seat and deforming vehicle
structure have different roles that work together.

M08-L02
Make the load part of the safety
check
Your goal: Distinguish weight terms and assess securing, capacity and trailer suitability.
Term
Meaning for this lesson
Tjänstevikt
Vehicle in its defined ready-for-use state; a car's figure includes the driver, while a

Registered maximum weight, built from the defined unladen/ready weight and

Actual weight transmitted to the road at that time.

Total weight minus the defined ready weight: the maximum passenger/cargo
load.
